people.name: Romulus
people.summary: Legendary founder and first king of Rome, son of Mars and the Vestal Rhea Silvia, suckled with his twin Remus by a she-wolf; tradition gives him a reign of 753-716 and a disappearance in a storm on the Campus Martius, after which he was worshipped as Quirinus.
people.detail: The twins legend is attested in Greek sources from the 4th-3rd century and monumentalised at Rome by the Ogulnii in 296. Romulus' 'institutions' (Senate of 100, curiae, the asylum, the rape of the Sabines, joint rule with Titus Tatius) are etiological reconstructions. Wiseman argues Remus was added in the 4th century to reflect patrician-plebeian power-sharing.
people.death: vanished in a storm during a review on the Campus Martius (legend); alternatively murdered by senators

people.name: Numa Pompilius
people.summary: Second king in the Roman tradition, a Sabine from Cures credited with founding Rome's religious institutions under the guidance of the nymph Egeria.
people.detail: The Calpurnii, Pomponii, Pinarii and Aemilii later claimed descent from his sons. The supposed 'books of Numa' discovered in 181 BC were burned as subversive.

people.name: Servius Tullius
people.summary: Sixth king, of slave or captive birth in Roman tradition and identified in an Etruscan tradition (Claudius' Lyons speech) with the adventurer Mastarna; credited with the census, centuriate assembly, tribes, the temple of Diana on the Aventine and a city wall.
people.detail: Murdered at the instigation of his daughter Tullia and her husband Tarquinius Superbus; Tullia drove her carriage over his body in the Vicus Sceleratus. The 'Servian' constitution as described by Livy is a 4th-3rd century system projected back. His patronage of Fortuna and Mater Matuta at the Forum Boarium (Sant'Omobono temples, 6th century) is archaeologically plausible.
people.death: murdered at the instigation of Tarquinius Superbus and Tullia

people.name: Tarquinius Superbus
people.summary: Seventh and last king of Rome in tradition, a tyrant who extended Roman power over Latium, began the Capitoline temple and was expelled c. 509, after which he sought restoration through Veii, Tarquinii, Porsenna and the Latins before dying in exile at Cumae.
people.detail: His reign shows Rome at its archaic peak: hegemony over Latium (reflected in the 509 Carthage treaty), colonies at Signia and Circeii, the Cloaca and Circus works, and the purchase of the Sibylline Books. The 'tyrant' portrait borrows from Greek models (Periander's poppy-lopping lesson to Thrasybulus reappears in the capture of Gabii).
people.death: died in exile at Cumae, at the court of Aristodemus

people.name: Lucretia
people.fullName: Lucretia, wife of L. Tarquinius Collatinus
people.summary: Roman matron whose rape by Sextus Tarquinius and subsequent suicide, after summoning her father and husband to swear vengeance, triggered the expulsion of the kings.
people.detail: Her story is a Roman exemplum of pudicitia and the paradigm of tyranny overthrown through outrage to a woman, repeated in Verginia (449). Livy's version dramatises it like a tragedy.

people.name: Lucius Junius Brutus
people.summary: Legendary liberator of Rome and first consul, Tarquin's nephew who feigned dullness (brutus) to survive, led the revolt after Lucretia's death, executed his own sons for plotting a Tarquin restoration, and died in single combat with Arruns Tarquinius at the Silva Arsia.
people.detail: The later plebeian Iunii, including Caesar's assassin, claimed descent despite the tradition that his only sons were executed; Dionysius notes the problem. His statue stood on the Capitol among the kings, holding a drawn sword.
people.death: killed in a cavalry duel with Arruns Tarquinius at the Silva Arsia

people.name: Tarquinius Collatinus
people.summary: Husband of Lucretia and colleague of Brutus as first consul; forced to resign and go into exile at Lavinium because he bore the hated name of Tarquin.
people.detail: His expulsion illustrates the archaic idea of a whole gens tainted by the regnum; Sp. Lucretius and then Publicola replaced him.

people.name: Publius Valerius Publicola
people.summary: Co-founder of the Republic, four times consul, who demolished his own grand house on the Velia when suspected of aiming at kingship, lowered the fasces before the people and is credited with the first law of appeal (provocatio).
people.detail: Plutarch paired him with Solon. The Lapis Satricanus (c. 500) naming the companions of 'Poplios Valesios' may refer to him. The Valerian family tradition, inflated by the annalist Valerius Antias, accounts for much of his legend.
people.death: died poor and was buried at public expense within the city

people.name: Lars Porsenna
people.summary: Etruscan king of Clusium who attacked Rome c. 508, nominally to restore Tarquin; Roman legend has him withdraw out of admiration for Roman heroism, but Tacitus and Pliny indicate he captured the city and imposed terms.
people.detail: Varro (in Pliny) described his fantastic tomb at Clusium with a labyrinth and pyramids, likely a fiction. His son Arruns was killed at Aricia by Latins and Cumaeans, ending his power in Latium.

people.name: Horatius Cocles
people.summary: One-eyed (cocles) hero who held the Pons Sublicius against Porsenna's army while it was demolished behind him, then swam the Tiber in armour.
people.detail: Polybius (6.55) tells a version in which he drowns, as an example of Roman self-sacrifice. A statue in the Comitium, probably of Vulcan or an unrelated lame figure, was explained by his story. Rewarded with as much land as he could plough in a day.

people.name: Mucius Scaevola
people.summary: Young Roman who infiltrated Porsenna's camp to kill him, stabbed the wrong man, and when captured thrust his right hand into a brazier to show Roman contempt for pain, earning the name Scaevola ('left-handed').
people.detail: The legend explained the cognomen of the plebeian Mucii Scaevolae, a great jurist family of the late Republic, and the 'Prata Mucia' across the Tiber.

people.name: Cloelia
people.summary: Roman girl given as hostage to Porsenna who led other girls in escaping across the Tiber; returned by Rome under the treaty, she was released by Porsenna in admiration with a group of hostages of her choosing.
people.detail: An equestrian statue of her stood at the top of the Sacra Via, a rare honour for a woman; it may originally have represented a goddess (Venus Equestris).

people.name: Aristodemus of Cumae
people.summary: Cumaean general who defeated the Etruscans in 524 and, leading the Cumaean contingent, destroyed Arruns Porsenna's army at Aricia c. 504; he then seized power as tyrant of Cumae and sheltered the exiled Tarquinius Superbus.
people.detail: Nicknamed Malakos ('the effeminate', or 'the soft'), he allegedly raised boys as girls to prevent a new aristocracy. He seized Roman grain ships in 492 as Tarquin's heir. Overthrown and killed by the sons of the exiles he had murdered. Dionysius' detailed narrative is thought to derive from a local Cumaean chronicle.
people.death: killed in an uprising of returned exiles
scholarship: Alföldi, Early Rome and the Latins (1965) 56-72

people.name: Aulus Postumius Albus
people.summary: Dictator who won the battle of Lake Regillus against the Latins (499 or 496), taking the cognomen Regillensis; he vowed the temples of Castor and of Ceres, Liber and Libera.
people.detail: His son dedicated the temple of Castor in 484. The Postumii were one of the great patrician houses of the early Republic.

people.name: Octavius Mamilius

roles.t: Leader (dictator?) of Tusculum and of the Latin League army

people.summary: Leading man of Tusculum and son-in-law of Tarquinius Superbus, who raised the Latin League against Rome and was killed at Lake Regillus.
people.detail: The Mamilii of Tusculum later became Roman citizens and reached the consulship (from 265). Their family legend traced them to Telegonus, son of Odysseus and Circe.
people.death: killed at the battle of Lake Regillus

people.name: Spurius Cassius
people.summary: Three times consul, author of the Foedus Cassianum with the Latins (493) and the treaty with the Hernici (486), dedicator of the temple of Ceres; condemned and executed for aiming at kingship after proposing the first agrarian law.
people.detail: His career is the centre of the 'adfectatio regni' pattern. That the later Cassii were plebeians while he was consul raises the question whether the early consulship was open to non-patricians.
people.death: executed for adfectatio regni (by the quaestors or by his father)

people.name: Coriolanus
people.summary: Patrician hero of the capture of Corioli (493) who opposed the plebs during the famine of 492-491, was exiled, and led the Volsci against Rome (c. 488) until his mother Veturia and wife Volumnia persuaded him to turn back.
people.detail: Livy reports conflicting traditions on his death: killed by the Volsci for his failure, or (Fabius Pictor) living on into old age in exile, lamenting that 'exile is more wretched for an old man'. Plutarch's life, the basis of Shakespeare's play, pairs him with Alcibiades. His historicity is doubtful.
people.death: uncertain: killed by the Volsci, or died in old age in exile
scholarship: Cornell, 'Coriolanus: myth, history and performance', in Braund & Gill (eds.), Myth, History and Culture in Republican Rome (2003)

people.name: Menenius Agrippa
people.summary: Consul of 503 who, according to tradition, ended the first secession by telling the plebs the fable of the limbs that starved themselves by refusing to feed the belly.
people.detail: The fable has Greek and Near Eastern parallels (Aesop, an Egyptian papyrus) and was probably attached to him later. He died so poor that the plebs paid for his funeral.
people.death: natural causes; buried at public expense

people.name: Appius Claudius Sabinus
people.summary: Sabine noble Attus Clausus of Regillum who migrated to Rome c. 504 with a large clientele, founded the patrician Claudii and as consul in 495 took a hard line against debtors.
people.detail: The archetype of Claudian arrogance (superbia) in Livy's portrayal of the family. His descendants include the decemvir (451), Caecus (312) and, through adoption and marriage, the emperors Tiberius and Claudius.

people.name: Cincinnatus
people.summary: Patrician called from his small farm across the Tiber to be dictator in 458, who rescued a consular army from the Aequi on the Algidus and resigned after sixteen days; dictator again at 80 in 439 during the Maelius affair.
people.detail: His poverty was explained by a heavy fine paid for his son Caeso, a violent opponent of the tribunes. He became the supreme exemplum of civic virtue for Romans and later for the American founders (the Society of the Cincinnati). The 458 narrative is legendary.

people.name: Appius Herdonius
people.summary: Sabine leader who seized the Capitol in 460 with some 2,500 exiles and slaves, calling slaves to revolt, and was killed when the Romans and Tusculans retook it.
people.detail: An example of the archaic condottiere with a personal war band, like Attus Clausus or the Fabii.
people.death: killed in the recapture of the Capitol

people.name: Appius Claudius the Decemvir
people.summary: Leading member of both decemvirates who drafted the Twelve Tables; in the second year his rule became tyrannical and his attempt to seize Verginia led to the decemvirs' fall.
people.detail: Livy portrays him as the archetypal Claudian tyrant. Whether the second decemvirate was really oppressive or became the scapegoat for the anti-plebeian conubium clause is debated.
people.death: suicide (or death) in prison awaiting trial

people.name: Verginia
people.summary: Plebeian girl whom the decemvir Appius Claudius tried to seize by having a client claim her as his slave; her father, the centurion L. Verginius, stabbed her in the Forum to save her honour, triggering the second secession.
people.detail: A conscious doublet of Lucretia, her story ends the decemvirate as Lucretia's ended the monarchy.
people.death: killed by her father in the Forum

people.name: Gaius Canuleius
people.summary: Tribune of 445 who carried the law allowing intermarriage between patricians and plebeians and campaigned to open the consulship to plebeians.
people.detail: Livy's speech for him (4.3-5) is one of the great set pieces on the equality of citizens, appealing to Rome's history of admitting outsiders (Numa, Tarquinius Priscus, Servius).

people.name: Spurius Maelius
people.summary: Wealthy plebeian eques who distributed grain during the famine of 440-439 and was killed by Servilius Ahala for allegedly plotting kingship.
people.detail: His razed house site, the Aequimaelium, remained an open space below the Capitol used as a livestock market. Cicero repeatedly cites his death as just tyrannicide.

people.name: Servilius Ahala
people.summary: Master of horse to Cincinnatus in 439 who killed Spurius Maelius in the Forum; exiled later for the deed according to some sources, then recalled.
people.detail: His dagger became a symbol of tyrannicide: Marcus Brutus, Caesar's assassin, displayed Ahala's portrait alongside L. Brutus' on his coins (c. 54 BC) through his Servilian mother.

people.name: Aulus Cornelius Cossus
people.summary: Patrician who killed Lars Tolumnius of Veii in combat and dedicated the second spolia opima in the temple of Jupiter Feretrius.
people.detail: Augustus' claim to have read 'consul' on Cossus' linen corslet served to deny the honour to M. Licinius Crassus in 29-27 BC.
scholarship: Rich, 'Augustus and the spolia opima', Chiron 26 (1996)

people.name: Lars Tolumnius
people.summary: King of Veii who encouraged Fidenae to revolt and whose order (or misunderstood dice-game remark) led to the murder of four Roman envoys; killed by Cossus in battle.
people.detail: A Tolumnius family is attested in Etruscan inscriptions at Veii (a 6th-century dedication by Karcuna Tulumnes in the Portonaccio sanctuary), which lends the name authenticity.
people.death: killed in single combat by A. Cornelius Cossus

people.name: Camillus
people.summary: Conqueror of Veii (396), exiled over the booty, recalled as dictator during the Gallic sack, and celebrated as 'second founder of Rome'; five times dictator and four times triumphator.
people.detail: His legend grew enormously, especially his rescue of Rome from the Gauls (unknown to Polybius) and his role in the compromise of 367. Much of the Camillus saga was shaped in the late Republic, perhaps with Sulla or Caesar in mind (Momigliano, Bruun). Plutarch's Life is the main narrative. He died in the plague of 365.
scholarship: Bruun, 'What every man in the street used to know: M. Furius Camillus, Italic legends and Roman historiography', in Bruun (ed.), The Roman Middle Republic (2000)

people.name: Brennus
people.summary: Chief of the Senonian Gauls who besieged Clusium, won at the Allia and sacked Rome; at the weighing of the ransom he threw his sword on the scales with the words 'vae victis'.
people.detail: The name may be a title or a borrowing from the Brennus who attacked Delphi in 279. Only Livy and Plutarch name him for 390.

people.name: Marcus Manlius Capitolinus
people.summary: Consul of 392 who, woken by Juno's geese, repelled the Gallic night attack on the Capitol; later champion of debtors, condemned for aiming at kingship and thrown from the Tarpeian Rock.
people.detail: His cognomen Capitolinus perhaps derived from his house on the Capitol rather than his heroism. The prohibition on later Manlii using the praenomen Marcus is attested.
people.death: executed by being thrown from the Tarpeian Rock
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. I (1997) 476-567

people.name: Titus Manlius Torquatus
people.summary: Won the torque of a Gallic champion in single combat at the Anio (361); as consul in 340 executed his own son for fighting against orders, then defeated the Latins at Vesuvius and Trifanum.
people.detail: 'Manliana imperia' became proverbial for harsh discipline. As a youth he had defended his father, L. Manlius Imperiosus, against a tribune by threatening him with a knife.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998)

people.name: Marcus Valerius Corvus
people.summary: Won his cognomen in a duel with a Gaul aided by a raven (349), won the first battles against the Samnites at Mount Gaurus and Suessula (343), calmed the mutiny of 342 and carried the lex Valeria of 300; consul six times between 348 and 299 and said to have lived to 100.
people.detail: Cicero (De Senectute) cites his 46-year span between first and sixth consulships and 21 curule offices as a model of active old age. The Valerian annalist Valerius Antias likely embroidered his career.
